messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Elena Weiss is a 73-year-old QA engineer who has spent decades building her life around precision, predictability, and control. In the first sessions, she described a childhood marked by physical abuse from a male caregiver she had depended on. What stands out in the way she tells it is how little narrative flow there is. She does not tell a story so much as produce stark, still images: his hand closing on her arm, the angle of a hallway lamp, dirt on the floor near a baseboard, the sharp shift in his body before he struck. At moments she can summon these scenes with photographic clarity, “like snapshots laid out in front of me,” but when asked to put them into words she falters, stares ahead, and says she knows exactly what happened yet cannot find language for it. At other times she recalls the same moments with a disturbing numbness, as though she were describing something that happened to another child. Even now, she returns to one unbearable conclusion: she was betrayed by someone she trusted, and she has never forgiven herself for not doing more to stop it.

Over the years, Elena came to believe that bad things happen without warning and that she cannot stop them. Uncertainty has become especially difficult for her. Once she was certain that danger announced itself only after it was too late, ordinary ambiguity started to snag her attention in a way it never had before. A postponed conversation, an unexplained change in a room, a man lingering in a doorway could all become charged because her own conclusions had taught her to treat uncertainty as a warning. When a meeting changed without explanation or a man in a dark suit came into view at a cemetery, the thought arrived almost with the sensation itself: this is what her life is, being caught off guard and unable to protect herself. Each reminder seemed to tell her again that she was still the child who had failed to stop what happened. If a meeting at work is moved without explanation, if her husband says, “We need to talk later,” if she does not know who will be present in a room, she feels a familiar drop inside her. Funerals and cemeteries are particularly potent. She avoids memorial services when she can, but when attendance feels unavoidable, the sight of men in dark suits standing quietly near graves can leave her feeling as if she is no longer fully in the present. Being alone with men is worst of all. Even now, when a male contractor lingers in an office doorway or a male colleague stays behind after others leave, her body reacts before she has had time to think; her shoulders harden, her breathing changes, and she begins scanning the room automatically.

Those triggers do not remain just moments of discomfort. In the office where she works as a QA engineer, she has become known for insisting on clear agendas, documented changes, and never being the last person in a conference room. She knows this sounds excessive, but uncertainty itself feels dangerous to her, and sudden movements by other people put her immediately on guard. When a younger male developer once reached across her desk quickly to point at a defect log, she jerked back before she understood why. In those moments she is superalert, watching hands, posture, exits, tone of voice. The physical alarm arrives first, and with it comes the old conviction that she is once again at the mercy of someone stronger, that she will not be able to stop what follows. Feeling her body surge like that has gradually become its own kind of proof for Elena that she is permanently vulnerable. The sheer force of the alarm convinces her, in the moment and afterward, that she is not someone who gets to feel safe.

The same situations also pull up memory. A cemetery service for an old neighbor recently brought back sharp visual fragments of childhood so vividly that she could see the gray cast of indoor light and the position of a man’s shoes on the floor, yet she felt detached and oddly blank while seeing it. What made those images grip so hard was the meaning she still gave them: proof that she had been helpless and had somehow failed. The more she returned to that conclusion, the more easily the old scenes came forward, as if her mind kept retrieving evidence for the case against her. When she is unexpectedly alone with a man, she may later find herself replaying isolated images rather than a continuous account, unable to explain to her husband why she is so shaken. Because these reminders are tied to betrayal and helplessness in her mind, they do more than evoke the past; they revive what she believes the past proved about her. She feels again that she failed to act, that she should have found some way to stop it, and the shame of that conclusion makes the memories harder to put into words, as if language itself stalls where blame begins.

That self-blame has narrowed her world. She increasingly arranges her workday to avoid uncertain encounters, asks to keep her office door open when male coworkers visit, and declines funerals with excuses about fatigue. Her husband has noticed that she studies unfamiliar men in restaurants and flinches at abrupt gestures. Elena understands that most of these people are not dangerous, but what frightens her most is how quickly her mind and body return to the certainty that danger is already here. Each fresh episode seems to confirm the belief that she is still vulnerable and still unable to protect herself, which leaves her feeling both ashamed and watchful.

She sought help after a funeral this spring. Standing near the grave, surrounded by grieving people, she became aware of a man moving in beside her and felt the old jolt surge through her before she could think. Later, trying to explain it, she could only produce disconnected visual details and then went numb. She told her husband she was tired of living as if the past could break through any ordinary moment. What she fears most is that she will spend the rest of her life braced for something she cannot prevent. What she hopes, cautiously, is to understand why these moments still have such power and to stop feeling that the frightened child in those images is all she has ever been.
